utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Djurdjic is questioning you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us take it slowly today so as to have everything recorded with as few corrections as possible. First I'd like to show you a document that we discussed yesterday. You already provided some answers to it, but I want to stay with it for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please receive document D003-2656.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this document is the rules of service of the VJ for 1996. Could you please read out paragraph -- or Article 473. It starts on this page and spills over onto the next.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Army units may be used to combat outlaw, sabotage, terrorists, and other enemy groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next page in the B/C/S. Eventually we'll have to change the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Or to prevent or eliminate a state of emergency by the state of the president of Yugoslavia or the Supreme Defence Council, the Chief of General Staff shall issue the order for the use of the army pertaining to this article. In case of an attack by an outlaw, terrorist, sabotage, or other armed enemy group at a unit or institution, the commanding or duty officer of the attacked unit, institution, or army facility shall immediately undertake the relevant defence and repelling measures and shall inform his superior thereof."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me that this encompasses two situations: One, when there is an attack; and the other, when the Chief of General Staff makes decisions even if there is no attack.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerns terrorist groups rather than an armed rebellion which was -- which prevailed in Kosovo in 1998. You will remember 1972 when a sabotage Ustasha group was introduced from Australia. That was the synonym that was frequently used for the sabotage terrorist groups from that point onwards. As regards Kosovo, we did not have a single terrorist group. We had what was basically an army there, the KLA. This was not an individual small group concerning which the Chief of the General Staff or the Yugoslav president could make decisions so as to avoid a state of emergency. But in 1998 as far as I know, there was a state of emergency. Everything was blocked, traffic, the territory, they established their own check-points, they mined roads. It didn't concern a single facility, say, in Drenica, but the entire territory of Kosovo. I believe that is why there was so much discussion about introducing a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You have embarked upon interpreting some legal regulations, but I would like to stay with the rules of service only for the time being. In the second part of this article, I believe the third paragraph, the issue is that of a unit reacting if exposed to an attack without any -- anyone's orders; am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to paragraph 1 of this article. I don't want to enter any legal debates with you or political debates, but when it says that the general or the Chief of the General Staff can use the armed forces pursuant to the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council and the president of Yugoslavia who presided over the Defence Council. In this article, there is no mention of a state of emergency; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are. However, it also says: "In order to prevent that a state of emergency comes about."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't think I find that in there. I can't see it. Yes, yes, "in order to prevent," you are right. Therefore it is possible under those conditions. And then we have paragraph 474 on the use of army -- no, no, that is irrelevant. Let's move on. General, you described your view of the KLA. I would like to know something more about the ways they were financed. Was that something that you were interested in in 1997, 1998, and 1999. When you took over duties, did you study that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not familiar with the way they were financed in the course of those few years, and there was no discussion about that when I came towards the end of April. Although I know what it used to be like preceding that period; therefore, I conclude that it was similar. First of all, they received donations collected by the Albanian lobby which was well off in financial terms abroad. There were various means of going about that. It even concerned stealing or robbery, and somewhere around 1985 or 1986, most of the money came from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the years immediately prior to the war and immediately after, were you familiar with any drug smuggling as being one of the basic sources of finance?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can make that conclusion. Drug trafficking is present even as we speak in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you took over your duties regarding the KLA, were you acquainted with the importance of foreign aid in terms of equipping and training the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not a topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many VJ former officers, as well as JNA former officers, were among the ranks of the KLA while you were on your duty?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not view that as a separate issue. What I knew was that they had some people from the JNA who joined the KLA. Basically, all of NCOs and COs who were the subjects of our investigations later on became KLA commanders. Basically all of them, and I have in mind around 15 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the period immediately prior to NATO bombardment and the stay of the Verification Commission, the OSCE, as well as KDOM, as well as the ways in which they overstepped the boundaries of their mandate by engaging in counter-intelligence activities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have mentioned already, I seem to remember that some members of that mission were in contact with KLA leaders, but nothing more specific than that. When I arrived at the service, I know I was briefed on that, and I remember that was from the period before I was reinstated. I also mentioned the photograph of Mr. Holbrooke with some KLA people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'd like to know what you know about the methods of operation of the KLA in terms of counter-intelligence. What was characteristic of that? I'm not so much interested in the military aspects, but the very nucleus of the problem in terms of abusing or misusing civilians. Did you have any information regarding that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The method of operation was that all reluctant Albanian population in Kosovo that did not line up, that did not rally around the KLA or any of its units, or who did not sign up to the KLA goals, or for whom there was even a shadow of a doubt that they were in one way or another loyal to the Serbian regime or were in contact with the security service, irrespective of the fact that they were ethnic Albanians, most of them were liquidated. They were treated extremely roughly. I know that some of our collaborators were eventually killed. That was quite common, and in such situations they simply put the ethnic affiliation aside. Another characteristic was that these terrorist armed groups mingled usually with local population. There were several such cases that we were briefed by various security organs, in the course of which we learned that fire was opened from say refugee columns on the police and the army. And then it was very difficult how to respond to that without suffering casualties, and at the same time not hurting in a sense civilians. I'm a bit familiar with the Albanian mentality since I have studied the problem for a long time. I learned that families, and entire parts of villages from which KLA terrorists hailed, moved together with them using them as a source of protection in the sense that they were protecting civilians. And at the same time, the civilians were there to make sure that no fire was opened at the KLA members. And they moved together as a single group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that on many occasions, the KLA operated wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. I don't know. I didn't pay attention to it. You know, a tradition in Albanians is that there must be a single rifle at least in every household hidden somewhere. So I cannot exclude the possibility that the civilians who were not officially or formally in KLA uniform and a KLA unit, that they opened fire as well. It was a general malaise. I don't know whether they changed clothes into uniforms, into civilian clothes, I don't know. I can tell you only about the methodology they used and their love of weapons. Almost all male Albanians irrespective of their age always kept a gun or a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A blood-feud has not been eradicated among the Albanian population, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'd like to know, Mr. General, is whether you have any knowledge about KLA members evacuating certain villages for their purposes in 1998, 1999, and during the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that as a general information, but I couldn't be specific which village suffered such a fate. But I know of this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to familiarise you with an exhibit P452. Rather, D452. No, it's P452.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, what we are about to see is a decision of the Chief of General Staff of the KLA Colonel Bislim Zyrapi, dated 1st April, 1999. Please pay attention to paragraphs 3 and 4, and tell us, was this one of the methods for the KLA to infiltrate the civilians while withdrawing from FRY forces?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it. I'm quite surprised that a person that I used to know, Bislim Zyrapi, became Chief of General Staff. Well, like commander, like army; he used to be an NCO in Sarajevo, and we used to deal with him in 1986. In the original text there are four 9s in the date, and the same has been reflected in the translation. What he drafted as Chief of General Staff is not of the same level of quality a JNA sergeant would draft. Well, this is not contentious that they moved the population in areas of combat operation, maybe for protection, but maybe for political interests. I cannot enter into speculation. But the fact stands that the population was moved around. From their perspective, maybe for protection. Women and children used to be in the woods and the western media took pictures of them representing them as displaced persons; but in professional terms we can deem that as evacuation, moving the population from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would like to go through some documents with you, but rather, let's finish with my yesterday's remark concerning the 25th of May document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be, I think, P -- 65 ter number 1459. 1459. That was 1459 in Milutinovic et al. We can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, let's take it from the top, from page 1. So the date is the 25th of May, 1999. You said that the long number reflects the 3rd Armies. Do you have the number of copies that this document was drafted in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be several copies, but no mark is borne by this document. Minimum number of copies to be drafted is two; one to the addressee, and the other for the archives of the drafter. You will see in other documents that this number of copies, if not indicated, doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, I agree with you. But this is a case where we have delivery order in terms of who should be -- who should receive that document. But let me ask you another thing, this was drafted by Mr. Pavkovic, bears his signature and the date, but you do not know whether he drafted that document on that date; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot say whether this was drafted on the date, but we can say whether it was entered into the log or the ledger on that date. The document might have been drafted a week prior to the date, but what is important is when it is registered in the ledger. On the 25th of May there is an addendum which is not usual. 94-1-2. What 94-1 is is worthy of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is stated in the stamp of this document, but whether it was registered or not can be determined only by gaining insight into the ledger?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Or if it was received by the General Staff and is addressed to the Chief of General Staff personally, then it should bear the stamp, the reception stamp; and this is why I said I could not testify whether this document reached the General Staff because there is no reception stamp of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, General. Let me ask you another thing. Is it true that all General Staff documents were placed into the military archive registered, recorded, and bearing military archive's stamps, so all General Staff documents are in the archives of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you about the exceptions. There were documents whose authenticity I have no reason to doubt, but which do not bear the archive stamp. It doesn't mean that all the documents must be in the archive, but the practice is whenever a document is archived or when documents are taken out of an archive, whoever is giving them away, they don't care whether -- who is going to do the triage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But if this document was received in the archive, then it should bear the archive's stamp. At least that was the practice in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your eagerness and enthusiasm is being reflected in the speed of your questioning. You are getting faster and faster, the interpreters are getting further behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. I'll be mindful of their needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So we've come to the importance of this document. Is this document of such a nature that it would be preserved by the General Staff had they received it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an individual issue. You may ask me whether I would keep it if I were Chief of General Staff, I would have. But I cannot enter into personal criteria. I know what you are interested in. Yesterday I explained quite clearly, the signature is that of the General Nebojsa Pavkovic. The part that bears the date 25th of May, this is drafted eight days after the briefing with the Chief of General Staff where he explains for the first time manifestations that are focused in an official document for the first time concerning problems with the relations with the MUP and conducts of some MUP elements. I told you that subsequently wrote what he should have written as early as April, and he is now seeking from the Chief of General Staff to resolve matters that is he could have resolved at the Joint Commission level in Pristina. I cannot tell you whether this document has been fortified by him and post-dated, and it was not drafted on the 25th of April, 1999, but 25th of April, 2001. You cannot ask me to explain that. What I've testified about are the facts which led to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are a fact witness, I'm going to use you as such and then we can later on determine whether some things are forgeries or not. You've disappointed me in another thing, I thought that the military followed rules and that there is a rule on archiving the documents, but I have that document so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to know about the contents; I'm interested in the very end of the document. I think that the contents are not credible. General, do you see who this document was delivered to? Is there a list of addressees?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the delivery order is. It is clear that it was delivered to the Chief of General Staff personally, that's at the beginning below the letterhead. Each document bears this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, General. One thing is who the document is addressed to, but the delivery order is an indication who should receive a certain document. And I've seen this in the military when you deliver documents through telex or teleprinter then there is a note "addressees," so this in my terms is the delivery order. We have the addressee on the first page, but we do not have any indication on how many copies are to be delivered to whom. It's usually customary to say one copy to security, one copy to department of this or that. This would be the delivery order. This is what I mean by delivery order.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right in this case. This document was delivered personally. And as head of the administration, or in other capacities, I also delivered -- I also received, personally delivered documents, which means they should be delivered personally to that addressee and to nobody else. And as I said yesterday, such a document is drafted in two copies. One copy stays with the author, and the other copy to the addressee. So there is no note to be delivered to this, that, and the other person. I've encountered many orders, particularly pertaining to the Joint Command without an indication of the addressees. Those documents had to be delivered to all units that were issued tasks in such an order, and they could be twenty. But it's certain that such a document was drafted in twenty copies and that each command had to receive copies; but documents drafted to be delivered to somebody in person, it doesn't bear at the end of document a note to be delivered to whom because it is stated in -- on the first page. Believe me, this is not the problem. The problem is, and as I testified in previous trial, is that it doesn't bear the reception stamp of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That as well may be, but as a soldier or a policeman, you had to verify to investigate a document, you see it was drafted but you have no indication of where it ended up in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are general security measures; I was counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. If this is true as General Pavkovic wrote in this document, and it was said that he had direct contact with Milosevic, hadn't he reported on these to Milosevic personally? Now he is writing to Ojdanic after all those meetings.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to go through the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No. What I'm interested in is the Pavkovic-Milosevic direct contact links.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist of what he described in terms of problems was referred to on the 16th of May to the Chief of General Staff and to President Milosevic on the 17th of May. But afterwards in this document he drafts a report where he covers his back and he is trying to find justification for some of the problems citing as reasons that MUP didn't want to cooperate and that they were not resubordinated. And now he is shifting the blame to the Chief of the General Staff and demands from the Chief of the General Staff to resolve those matters together with President Milosevic. This is one level. So he drafted this document to justify his omissions in April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to say another thing. If he had direct links and contacts with Milosevic, he could have briefed Milosevic orally about these problems. He did not have to brief anybody else if Milosevic was deciding on everything; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he communicated with Mr. Milosevic in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have the following document under 65 ter; it is 4017.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And these now, General, are the minutes from the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff, the senior staff meeting. So may we have your comments to this first document, please. There are several that I'd like us to look at, but this is the first collegium. Would you explain to us something about this collegium of the General Staff, when General Ojdanic was there; and do you recognise this general form, the way it's set out, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read this document carefully, or rather, the minutes from this particular collegium, both from the aspects of learning something that I didn't know when I had retired, because this is strictly confidential. Everything discussed at this highest level is strictly confidential, so I was curious to see what it said, to read the document. And what I can tell you first of all is that minutes of this kind were kept during the JNA, when I was in the JNA myself and when I took part in the work of the collegium. Then we can see that it is a tape recording, that it was the transcription of a tape recording which means that the same practice was applied that had existed in the JNA, that is to say that important collegium meetings were recorded, that was compulsory, and that they were supposed later on. So from the aspects of how this was done, what it looks like, and how the discussion of the participants was done, I think that it is authentic and correct. Now, part of the collegium of the General Staff after the theft of the documents - and I'm sure you know about this - it was processed by -- well, Vlajkovic was involved because he disclosed a military secret and he received part of the minutes from the collegium unlawfully. And this was -- he was prosecuted later on. He published it in a book, and then he cave one example to General Perisic, and he in turn sent it on to the US intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what about Milos Ladicorbic, captain of this ship, what was his specialty?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when he was in the security section of the navy -- well, he was in the security section of the navy and then moved to the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: He says here -- do you know about this actually? That's what I'm asking you. I know you were already a pensioner, but you might have had some contact with him. Anyway, the situation with the respect to the NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not objecting, I think maybe something was lost in the translation. It seems as if Milos was mentioned earlier and, well, that was lost in the translation because I think counsel's reference to Milos is said in such a context that it suggests to me that there was a mention of the Milos earlier in the evidence or by counsel and we missed it. So it's just difficult to follow. I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The cause of the problem, Mr. Djurdjic, is that you can't wait for the witness's answer to finish to come in with your next question and the interpreters are still some way behind. So they miss things. Perhaps you better clarify this a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, bravo, colleague Stamp; you're quite right. You're right, Your Honours, I will do that. Let me ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I asked you was this: Can you tell us, this man, captain of the -- Milos Ladicorbic, what was his specialty, what did he deal with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that previously he was in the security organs, that I knew him personally, and afterwards he moved to the military intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, at this time, at the end of 1998 and beginning of 1999, did you have any information about the ground forces, the land forces of NATO packed in Macedonia and Albania, what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did know as much as any citizen knew from the media. I knew that there were those forces over there and that they were grouping and concentrating forces and that there were NATO bases over there, although they weren't constituted in that way and perhaps referred to in that way, but those forces did exist over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me, Lieutenant-General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, were you on good terms with him? Did you have any knowledge about him? And we can move on if not.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm waiting for you to complete your question. Yes, I was on good terms with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we look at page 6 of the B/C/S, and that would be page 7 of the English, para 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that should be the address made by Mr. Dimitrijevic when he took the floor. Did you discuss anything with respect to para 2 on the Serbian page about verifications that the KLM could know what the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: KVM. Interpreters correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you included in any of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was waiting for the document to come up on my screen. Yes, I've read it now. Well, it's like this: We didn't discuss this topic. We discussed other subjects. However, as I knew General Dimitrijevic and as I knew the circumstances and the situation, I don't think there's anything to be challenged here with respect to what he said. And that he had good information, valid information, because he had good information sources and he knew what was going on in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we have page number 8 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And would you take a look at para 2 which begins on the following page. In English it is page 8, para 3, from the top.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again let me repeat, I didn't discuss any of this with anyone. However, I do know from the entire story and the general mood that prevailed that everything that is stated here was reflected the actual situation and the -- that the mission was objective. So they had detailed information, detailed information about facilities with all the coordinates, that is to say, the OSCE. Not only down there in Kosovo, but the intelligence organs had very precise information and detail. So they knew where the zero-point of an explosion was. They knew this in Belgrade and so on. And with the GPS they had all this information, all the coordinates; they had them in front of them on the table, so they knew all the military facilities, the civilian facilities, their importance, and all the rest of it. So they were extremely well informed about the targets that needed to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move on to the time when you were re-activated, so tell me what you know about that from your service once you were re-activated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I make a joke. Everything had already been destroyed by that time, if I can say so, the General Staff buildings in Belgrade, and the bridges, and all the rest of it. So there were several cases which were uncovered and documented and the perpetrators were arrested, I don't want to mention their names now because some of them have some official functions now. But when I arrived, it was the stage at which all the information had been collected about the effects of their actions. So all the facilities were filmed and recorded. And where they weren't satisfied with the results they had achieved, they would repeat their actions. And this true of the General Staff building; there was one hit to begin with, and then afterwards, we uncovered several days later that is, a man who had filmed it all from the Beogradjanka high-rise building. So he filmed the results of that first impact and then there was the second hit and the second impact. So it was a stage in which in fact they were finishing off, if I can use the term, finishing off what they failed to achieve previously. And as you know, I arrived on the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't just mean about the bombing. What happened on the ground, what did NATO do there? The representatives of the various states and your intelligence information about them and experience with them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ever since I worked in the intelligence organs, intelligence service for 30 years, we always knew what kind of individuals were in charge of collecting all intelligence on a given territory and setting the targets, indicating the targets. And every time they would engage in reconnaissance work, intelligence reconnaissance of course once again, repeated action, they would activate the situation, or rather, that means they would update the changes that had taken place on the ground. And that's where we engaged in specific warfare where we would serve up erroneous information and things like that. But it was a continuous activity which is ongoing to the present day, that is, the task of the intelligence services to gather information about potential targets which might come in use at some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, I wasn't thinking of the bombing, I was thinking of the situation on the ground in Kosovo. Did they enter into the FRY, or where were they? I'm asking you as of the 27th of April, that is to say, after you arrive.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any foreigners of that nature, they engaged in reconnaissance work from the air and used the information they collected. They had drones flying and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly refrain from overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, before I forget, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there's also the regulation that was used earlier, rules of service, I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that part of an exhibit we've already received or not, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Thank you, Mr. Stamp. First of all, the rules of service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's happening, we'll receive the minutes of the collegium, which haven't been tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document bearing 65 ter number 4017 will become Exhibit D166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the rules of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was D003-2656, of the Army of Yugoslavia. Yes, indeed, of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That means it's not an exhibit in our trial yet. We will receive that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will become Exhibit D167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, were you re-activated when the three members of the US Army were captured in -- was it on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija? I believe so.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of that case, it was somewhere down from Macedonia, but it happened before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were there any developments while you were in service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, do you happen to remember that other incident linked to a humanitarian worker who was from Price or whatever -- Prite, Prite [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that he was engaged in intelligence gathering. The two or three cases he was one of them, and I think there was some links to the Australian Embassy, unless I'm very much mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I wanted to ask you, In your counter-intelligence work, did you have any information about whether there were members of NATO, any NATO people in the staffs and units of the KLA? Did you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether there were any Mujahadeen or other foreigners in KLA units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's a book I have read recently by an American lecturer at their naval academy John Simber [phoen], I think, and he discusses that in detail. I also something about that from the time of my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a thing or two about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are discussing this book which has recently been translated into Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just stay with the information that the services had. Let's keep away from books.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book confirms some information. In the period between the 27th of April and until the end of the war, we didn't have much time to deal with al-Qaeda. But I do know that al-Qaeda had its presence in Kosovo throughout that time and that it arrived there from Bosnia. They simply moved some al-Qaeda activists. But I can't give you any precise names though. In any case, there were several cases detected confirming al-Qaeda presence within the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I am a interested in whether you received such security related information from your junior security organs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I toured my security organs, no one briefed me on that specifically, probably because it was no longer an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see Defence Exhibit D003-3134.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is also from a collegium of the General Staff. Is this the right format?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The format is correct. At least the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit D168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could with have D003-2662 next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on what I can see, I can only repeat the previous comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have not yet seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 003-2662. It should be the minutes of the 17th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 4th session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are confused by the numbering here. The English number is quite different from the original. Is it the correct English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can see that the 17th of December is also mentioned in the English, and it is certainly there in the Serbian. It is 1998, the ministers collegium, Biljana Popovic was the typist. I'm not sure what is the number you are referring to. Copy is number 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my number is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, we are told that it is the correct document, the English translation has a quite different number and that was giving us concern. So this will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit D169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have D003-3134 next. It should be dated the 14th of December. Did we already have that? Oh, well, then all three ... The first one was 10 December, then 14 December, and the 17th of December. If this one was already admitted, D003-3134, then I would ask for the assistance of the court clerk.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, concerning these collegium meetings, this would be it. I will raise an issue later concerning the second session. Next could we please have D003-3085.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's nothing to comment on. Everything is in there. This came from the intelligence administration. It would be particularly interesting if they had captured any of these persons, but as far as I know they never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was your task to capture them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were writing about this and always on the basis of the information we had, and they don't specify which available information it was. Usually one would have a coded source name and an assessment of accuracy, as well as the reliability of the source. Each such document is filled out by an operative, but this is merely an information from the field. I can neither deny or confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the format, is this familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite familiar with the way operatives reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit D170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D003-3087.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, again, I'm only interested in the format.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the format is the same, and it was signed for Branko Krga, he was not person signing it, although that is not important. They were specific in one thing, they had this particular number of 1, 2, 3, 4; but it was not part of the ledger such as would be customary for the security administration. They merely had reports number this and that. They would start with the first report that year and then end with the end of the year and this would be their typical way of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do see a ledger number on the top.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different thing. That is the intelligence department which received that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Explain me this please, these numbers are the numbers of reports forwarded to the Chief of Staff, this report number 37 for example.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report number drafted by the intelligence administration based on the influx of information from the field. We would put in the contents and then say what the report refers to. It would describe the problem in short terms, and then it is registered in the intelligence department of the General Staff under this number, 06, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have D003-3089 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Again, only the format, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same. I'm also trying to compare the number of the report and connect that to the date, and indeed the previous number preceded this one in terms of date. There is also the stamp of the archive there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I'd like to have D003-3091, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we come to the 3rd of April. Is this still the same template?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still waiting for it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what it says underneath the stamp or below it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Distribution, commands of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army and to the operational strategic formations. I don't want to comment on the work of the military security service the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Intelligence service. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they used different methods. In any case, they were forwarding information and with we were supposed to verify it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The report of the 13th of April, 1999, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report will become Exhibit D173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next let's have D003-3093, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a full report as opposed to the short telegraph reports that can be sent a few times a day that we just saw. This report collates the information collected from different sources. I only had time for a very brief cursory look. In any case, this is a report on the use of depleted uranium projectiles. I do see, however, that the report refers to several sources, something concerning Germany, and then the international activity centre, and certain locations where we had operatives abroad. They forwarded this information to the intelligence administration which in turn drafted this report. Based on such a report, the General Staff can -- unless sending it directly to the commanders of strategic formations -- can issue an order from the General Staff or the Supreme Command staff towards subordinate commands, letting them know about such occurrences. I see there the stamp of the military archives, and I believe this is a fully, accurate, and true report. Authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, as of the moment you were re-activated on the 27th of April and until the end of the war, did you have any information or knowledge on the use of such means at Pastrik and Kosare?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was in the ABHO branch, the nuclear and chemical warfare branch, I see that there is a mention of it there requiring that a scouting patrol be sent out in the field, and we even after the war found traces confirming that such ammunition was used and some Italian KFOR members suffered certain symptoms as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, the report of the 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we see D003-3096.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we switch to the last page, I'm interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, shall we turn to the second page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is dated 4th of May, 1999, at that time you were active duty. Let's go back to page 1, please. Paragraph 2 is what I'm interested in, and the whole of paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th of May, isn't it, I was in Montenegro on that day. Well, this is the type of report that intelligence administration sends summing up the developments in a preceding period, organising them into paragraphs, as you can see them. These are sent to commanders of operative strategic groups, commanders of 1st, 2nd, 3rd Army, navy, air force, et cetera. This is used to assess the situation and it to supplement some orders in terms of what may happen. I see that they make mention that information received through agents, through operational means as they put it, and the intelligence department had their agents. We in the security administration before and during that period, and after, we would read or not read such reports. We had a problem where we received a large quantity of information from the ground. We would leaf through such reports, but it would not specifically concern us in terms of that we should act upon it. This as you can see is delivered to operative strategic group commanders. You see that there were calculation -- or speculations about the aggressors' attack, the axis of attacks, et cetera. Everything had been done in the military to resist that land invasion. Particularly in the area of Kosovo, you know, the defence lines were firm and they never invaded Kosovo. But this report highlights possible routes of axis from Montenegro, Albania, Macedonia, so this information as far as I can say it reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's tender this document, please. It was report number 73 from the 4th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to play general because we are going to see a strategic document later on. But let me ask you, you know that the KLA performed on the 9th of April a land invasion from Albania between Morina and Kosare, it lasted for almost 2 months?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is no doubt an operation by the KLA, they received support and help and assistance in that area. Let me remind you that on the 1st of June when I attended a meeting of the Joint Command in Pristina when General Pavkovic briefed us that forces are grouped in Albania numbering 2.000, fighters along a 6 kilometre stretch of the frontline, which is a high concentration of troops, and being supported by air force, this was nothing new. Such groups equipped and armed were infiltrated from Albania throughout the time. But there were several stages planed for the execution of that operation. This is now a stage where, since they hadn't succeeded in destroying military facilities and military targets, then the intelligence notifies us that they are going to progress to another stage and that would be attacks against military target --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Civilian targets. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- civilian facilities, bridges, trains. There was a train hit in the south of Serbia once. I believe it reflected their anger and wrath since they had not achieved their military targets, reckoning that the morale of the military and the civilians would be destroyed, and what I -- what they said was borne true later on in April and May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of June or the end of May, a second axis of invasion through Pastrik was used?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, attacks were constant and continuous. I never grouped them along axis. Most probably you can find information about that in those military documents. Since this is my testimony, give me some liberty. I've read these documents, they are many documents which can be used by the Prosecution and the Defence, and it's just a matter of who is going to use them best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe this is the right time for a technical break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness comes, I would like to move about an issue to the benefit of the expediency of the trial. It seems that both the Prosecution and the Defence have problems in terms of adducing military documents. And I thought, since I do have the intention of using them -- those documents, but since they are of the same format and they are numerous, it would be ridiculous for me for use 20 or 30 minutes of the collegium meetings and orders - there's a large number of them used by the Prosecutor - it would it be ridiculous for each of them to tender during court time. And why don't we admit them in batches if they are not contentious so that we don't have to go through each and every one of them with the witness. That would be my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It sounds a sensible idea. It is exactly the sort of thing that ought to be decided by agreement between the counsel and would save a lot of time, and we would encourage counsel to reach agreement about those documents. We will facilitate any such agreement. Thank you Mr. Djurdjic. Now, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's digress a bit to conclude an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D104.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've seen this document, and you've seen the document following it. You know the document 105 is a supplement to this order, so you are familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the last page of this order signed by the Joint Command. And in the same document -- of the Pristina Corps, in the supplement to this decision, that supplement bears the signature of the commander of the Pristina Corps, Major-General Vladimir Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right saying based on the basis of those two documents it is evident that decision-makings and maps, that everything was produced at the level of the Pristina Corps. With the difference being that sometimes it was signed by the joint commander and sometimes when, in haste, it would bear the signature of the commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't comment on that. All the document that is I've seen and that bear the phrase "Joint Command," they do not bear the signature of the commander of that command or any other commanders, but just -- there is an indication of the Joint Command standing behind that. And the ledger for such documents was kept at the Pristina Corps Command, and those documents bear the same indication as combat documents and orders of the Pristina Corps commander, that indication being 455, dash, and then the number of the document in the sequence of their production. But when in haste, they would just put "Joint Command" in place of the signature. As I've already explained, what was labelled Joint Command were people occupying the most responsible positions and the highest positions. They would hold a briefing on the most important developments of the day, and then agree on an order or a decision for the next day. In case where things were verified by the commander of the 3rd Army, MUP generals, and Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic, when nothing is contended, then such documents would further be elaborated by the Pristina Corps. But since the preliminary decision was taken on a session of the Joint Command, then the signature would bear the phrase the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. Have you noticed if there is any difference -- But firstly let's deal with this: Ledger was kept in a chronological order, the ledger of the Pristina Corps, do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Furthermore, have you noticed any difference up to the moment of the decision on resubordination, how many decisions had been signed by Joint Command, and what -- and the period after that order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't analysed that particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excellent. You know grammar well, and when you read the decisions and orders of the Joint Command, doesn't it seem to you that one of the same organ is issuing orders to another subordinate organ to cooperate and support another organ particularly for 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's strange. A document and an order of the Joint Command is produced in essence by the commander of the Pristina Corps, thereby issuing himself orders taken by that Joint Command. It's most probably complicated to understand what was going on. As I've explained, on the basis of what I saw at that meeting on that day, what was discussed and deliberated on that meeting, they would go to have lunch or dinner, and the person staying behind to formulate that into an order or a decision is the Pristina Corps commander and his staff, and most probably somebody from MUP had to do the same for their purposes. I can tell you almost each document may bear the indications of either the Pristina Corps or the Joint Command; all of them are strictly formulated from paragraph 1 to paragraph 13 or 14, drafted obviously by military professionals and not civilians because there were civilians and other personnel in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not doubting or questioning the professional manner in which those were drafted, but I'd like to ask you as a general and a security officer, and I know that you know other regulations. In normal times, in peacetimes, without an order on resubordination, without any state of emergency, is it possible for a military unit to issue decisions and orders to gendarmerie or MUP units to follow that order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can. If that unit had been empowered and if that other unit had been resubordinated to it. So it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, but there's no resubordination, no order on that situation and the state is normal. In such circumstances, can a military unit issue an order to use a gendarmerie unit or a MUP unit, or conversely, if it's possible in peacetime without any state of emergency or state of war, a MUP unit command a military unit to do something?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are of the same rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can they perform the same functions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is what they insisted on the 9th of July meeting that everybody should mind their own business.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May counsel slow down a bit because they are overlapping, please. Could counsel kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, if both the army and the police are expected to act, then, in the typo, the heading, it always says Joint Command without a signature?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand you. I don't follow you. What is it that you are asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is what I want to ask you. There's no extraordinary state, there's no decision on resubordination. It is obvious that these orders in 1998 right up until the decision on resubordination in 1999 are brought so that the police and army can work together. Now, since there's no such decision, then both the army and the police could act - could they not? - because they have the army units and police units under them and they are contained in this order, and it says Joint Command because under the law they can't issue orders to each other and deploy them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm coming to my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: "Am I right in saying... " -- that is what my question was going to be. Am I right in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you are right, no. And here is why: You are going to find documents of the Joint Command and after the war officially began and a state of war officially proclaimed, you'll once again have, well, not only in 1998, but also in 1999 there are orders of the Joint Command. And I noticed that there are the code signs and signals with respect to radio communication and so on, so you are not right in my opinion. You can't interpret it that way. That is my opinion on the basis of all the documents that I've looked through that just because of a fact that an emergency state had not been proclaimed whereas objectively on the ground two are parallel armed forces were being -- were going into action, the army and the MUP, that something should have existed as a Joint Command to issue orders to both these entities. So what is called Joint Command, this Joint Command still didn't have its staff, and that's where it differs to, for example, 1972 when the group was infiltrated in Radosa, a sort of Joint Command was established made up of the MUP, and the army, and the Territorial Defence, and police, and politicians, and state officials, and so on and so forth. But somebody has to stand at the head, controlling the overall activities. And here, I would say that this was more -- well I saw it more as a staff which is there to coordinate something. They had very little to do in the military sense by way of issuing orders and compiling documents; but the most responsible persons would sit down together, decide what they were going to do in the coming period, or what was to be done in the coming period, and then General Lazerovic who attended the meeting was given the assignment of putting that into practice. And now he's writing, and it says the Joint Command, and he is in this paradoxical situation in which he himself, in para 5, issues an assignment to himself, an assignment to the Pristina Corps. Or rather in para 4, he makes a decision as commander of the Pristina Corps, which in fact should be a decision made by the Joint Command and taken by the Joint Command. So what I'm saying is this: And I stand by what I say, 1998 was not only a year in which documents appear with Joint Command on them. We had them in 1999 and even at the time when resubordination took place under the law and so on and so forth. But in Kosovo in 1998 as well - and you quoted yourself that article, I think it was 173 from the rules of service of the Army of Yugoslavia - once the army is being deployed and always when the army is being deployed in a particular zone or area, everything taking place and acting in that zone objectively is under the de facto command of the army. So you can't have two commanders in one zone. And the rules of service of the Army of Yugoslavia stipulate that the military commander is in fact the commander in a situation of that kind. So even when there is no state of emergency, although these are two parallel organs, there is synchronization where in fact one of them has to command -- is in command of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the first point that I'd like you to tell me is that after the 18th of April, the major part of the orders come from the Pristina Corps, and they are far less titled Joint Command. But let's leave that alone for the time being, it's not a question for you. Let's move on to another area. To something else. But let me say that I'm quite sure that not a single military unit can act pursuant to an order from the SUP of Pristina; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no it can't; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to another area, General. Since you became re-activated and informed of the situation and acquainted it, did you ever hear about a plan for ethnic cleansing of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the assumption that such a plan existed at a state level, would at that time the Supreme Command staff had have to have been informed of a plan of that kind had it existed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: It's all speculation now and assumption. Firstly, let me say that I don't think the best term is "plan for ethnic cleansing." I don't think that's a proper phrase. It would be a more correct to say a decision to implement ethnic cleansing. Now, faced with that kind of situation, you wouldn't have to write any document and then devise a plan and say in the first ten days, Let's deal with these three villages, for example. What we are talking about here is whether a decision was ever made and whether this process evolved on the ground according to somebody's decision up there or whether it was spontaneous and whether that was reacted to or not. So those are all the theories and speculations. But let's stay with your question. First of all, had that come to the General Staff, I'm sure that the Chief of the General Staff, because I knew him personally as a human being, he would have reacted to it, and he would ask to have been received by the supreme commander to clear this up and say that the army is not there to do things like that. So no such plan existed. No such order existed in the General Staff, at least I don't know about it. But when I was in the field for those seven day, when I was in Kosovo, then I had -- they were -- people reported to me and briefed me about certain activities that were taking place down there, people being expelled from their homes, but that transports were being organised or people loaded up or the times of departure and so on set. I really don't know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've come to the area of your practical work. Down the security chain of command, did you have intelligence and information telling you that organised or any other kind of expulsion of the Albanian population was being conducted by the FRY?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no knowledge about that, that this was done by the authorities and the knowledge of the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. However, I've always -- I've already given you examples of people being expelled. And one such example was in Kosovska Mitrovica. That's one case. But I know of another case too where a column of some kind, a column of refugees moving from Kosovo towards Montenegro, that behind this group of -- this -- of the population, and I can't say whether there might have been any terrorists or armed persons in that column, anyway, they were being expelled up to Rozaj to Montenegro. It wasn't a document in the Slobodan Milosevic trial; it wasn't exhibited because it wasn't in the indictment, the area of Montenegro. Now, the other case I know of was that the MUP asked why the organs of the army were turning back columns from the border, and there were reactions to that. So that's another case in point. So these -- this one group was moving out, and I'm not saying whether the MUP was at their rear; there were people who fled from Kosovo -- most of the people were fleeing from Kosovo just as they fled from Belgrade during the bombing for instance. However, the question is why the army was stopping them at the border and sending them back, and I can only conclude that it was welcome that they were leaving. Now, the next part, why at the border, were these people who were going out -- complete -- entire families, I'm not saying whether there were terrorists among them who had changed their clothing, anyway, all these people were leaving, they were going out, taking all their personal documents, their IDs, and everything that later on could prove that they were who they were if they wanted to return. So those are three parameters that I as a human being would like to present to you regardless of how anybody is going to interpret it. So I draw the conclusion from that that there were phenomena of that kind. But as to any decision that that should be done, I do not know of any such decision especially not with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And do you know that there was a decision made that this should be tolerated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no discussion or decision at all. Nothing at all. There wasn't any meeting that I attended when this question of the people's departure was raised and discussed or the fleeing of Albanians to -- from Kosovo to Montenegro, Albania wherever; and then we put this on the agenda to say whether we're going to stop this or not. No, it was just what happened on the ground down there, and there was no reaction in any organised form.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down and refrain from overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you inform anybody about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where and when and whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of May when -- or rather, 8th of June when I returned from touring Kosovo, we wrote a piece of information about all the crimes and all everything that was going on, this was handed over to the chief of the administration Geza Farkas, and then he handed that document over to the Chief of the General Staff, and he handed it over in turn to Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you'll have to pause. You come straight in at the end of a long answer and it gives the interpreters no chance to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- well, I seem to be doing all sorts of things here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you complete your answer? You gave the document to Geza Farkas, and he handed it over to the chief the General Staff, and then it went up to Slobodan Milosevic; was that the end of your answer? Had you completed your answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You have nothing further to add?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after that, I left. I went to Nis to organise security measures for pulling the army out of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I just wanted to make sure that I hadn't cut you off in your answer. I just wanted to ask you now that you mentioned you're going down there and receiving information, the information that you received, you received it from the security office on the ground. Now, do you know later on whether that information was checked out and verified, the information that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the chief of security attending those meetings, of the 3rd Army that is, Colonel Antic from Nis, when we returned to Belgrade we had a meeting in Nis on our way back, and I gave him the task of looking at everything that we had observed down there, and all the notes I made in my working diary, that he should turn this into an official document, file an official document on the basis of that. And as far as I know, that's what he did. Now, with respect to verifying the information and data. Perhaps the most characteristic piece of information is the one in Kosovska Mitrovica. I didn't issue the task of that being checked out because ultimately it wasn't a problem that was linked to the army. It was the problem that we came across as it stood as a byproduct, if I can use that phrase, of the work of an intelligence officer in Prizren. So I didn't order that information of that kind be checked out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D003-2985.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing before I move on to this document. General, when one loses an ID or a passport, what do you do?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I report that to the organs of the MUP to be issued with a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct that registers are kept in terms of all citizens of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether all registers, birth registers, death registers, and registers of citizenship were preserved and still exist in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were moved. I have some family members born in Gnjilane and they are now being issued with new passports. They need to get their original documentation in Vranje because that's where their registration was moved to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that most of the Albanians, after the 26th of June, came to Serbia to be issued with ID cards and passports before the KFOR documents were introduced?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By virtue of losing a document, can one lose one's identity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are still waiting for D003-2985.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we will move to directives. If I understood properly, these are strategic documents; we see one such document dated the 28th of July 1998. It is a General Staff of the Yugoslav Army directive. Can you please comment briefly on this directive.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I can see on the screen, which is the first page, which is in full accordance with standard templates with standard procedure, to tell you anything more, I would have to read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have you not had opportunity to see this document during your proofing?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the Roman numeral I, we see information about the enemy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then if we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As you can see, the last page contains some information about an attachment on the strength of combat groups. Am I right that the directive was signed by the Chief of the General Staff, Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At the end of the directive, we see in how many copies it was printed, and who it was distributed to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into any deeper discussions about this directive, but let me ask you this: Did you know at the time that according to the military information, KLA held over 30 per cent of the territory?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at that time or at the period preceding that the road Pristina-Pec was blocked, as well as the road Pristina-Prizren?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
